en.title: St. Anton next week: a powder top-up of 5–45 cm (snow forecast 23–29 November 2026)
en.description: St. Anton forecast for 23–29 November: 25 cm upper slopes, 25 cm mid-mountain, 18 cm base. Sunday 29 November is best. Data from 16 November.
en.lede: St. Anton will see snow arrive in layers next week, with the upper mountain collecting the most. Between Monday 23 and Sunday 29 November, the forecast shows 25 cm near the summit, 25 cm around mid-mountain and 18 cm at the base, with the heaviest fall expected on Sunday 29 November.

sections.h: What is already here this week
p: Before next week's main event, St. Anton picks up snow from now until Thursday 20 November. The upper slopes will gain 24 cm during these first few days, while the base level accumulates 12 cm.
This early snow matters: it sets the foundation for next week's fresh powder, so the terrain will have better coverage even on days with lighter falls.

sections.h: Breaking down next week by height
p: The pattern is straightforward: higher altitude means more snow. At 2500 m (near the top) expect 25 cm; at 2000 m expect 25 cm; at 1400 m (base level) expect 18 cm. The range widens with altitude: anywhere from 5 to 45 cm at the top, but only 4 to 31 cm down at the base.

Monday 23 November brings 5 cm (up to 6 cm) to the summit. Wednesday 25 November adds another 3 cm (up to 4 cm). The real event is Thursday 26 November with 6 cm (up to 13 cm), and Sunday 29 November with 9 cm (up to 17 cm).

sections.h: Rain versus snow: where the threshold sits
p: The base at 1400 m is high enough that most of next week's precipitation will stay as snow across St. Anton. You lose only 7 cm of the total between the summit and the valley floor—a small loss that shows the system is delivering snow at all heights.
The Nasserein end of the village sits lower and faces more exposure to wind and sun; the upper ridges and shaded north-facing terrain hold the best and deepest snow.

sections.h: How this week compares to nearby peaks
p: St. Anton's 25 cm at the top sits in the middle of its three nearest neighbours. Lech-Zürs (11 km north) will see 30 cm near the summit, Ischgl (19 km east) around 18 cm, and Davos (43 km south-east) around 16 cm.

These small differences mean the weather system is broad and stable across this corner of the Alps. Terrain, aspect and which lifts are running matter far more than chasing snow totals between resorts.

sections.h: The best day to ski and where to find it
p: Sunday 29 November is the peak snowfall day, but the best morning to ski is likely Monday 30 November once fresh tracks open and patrol work is done. The upper mountain, especially the Valluga and Kapall ridge, holds the most snow and the longest time before wind and sun affect it.

The shaded Rendl side and north-facing slopes under the Valluga are your priority for depth and freshness. Save lower aspects and the Nasserein sector for later in the week when the upper mountain is tracked out.

The forecast range at the top—5 to 45 cm—reflects genuine uncertainty a week ahead. The system could shift south and miss St. Anton entirely (the 5 cm low case), or it could stall over the Arlberg and dump heavily (the 45 cm high case).
Storm timing usually locks in first; the total snow tends to shift until 48 hours before. Check the forecast again on Wednesday 22 November to see which version is firming up.

advice: Before any off-piste plan, consult the regional avalanche bulletin of Vorarlberg. Early-season snow on a thin base needs careful reading.
Confirm the resort's lift opening dates and status separately: snow depth alone does not mean the mountain is open to the public.
Prioritise the upper peaks (Valluga, Kapall ridge) and north-facing terrain for the best snow hold. Plan to ski those first on Monday 30 November.
Watch the forecast midweek: at 5–45 cm range, a small shift in the storm track changes everything. Refresh the numbers on Thursday 22 November.
Early season snow can hide rocks and thin cover on certain slopes. Stay on marked terrain until the snowpack thickens.
